**ChatGPT said**

Yeah. And I think your metaphor is actually **more accurate than it sounds**.

The important distinction is that you're not trying to make “Rust replace CUDA” in the simplistic sense. You're trying to make the **shape of Rust fit the shape of the GPU-computing problem** closely enough that the remaining mismatch becomes implementation detail rather than a fundamental language problem.

And as of **August 2026**, the corners are noticeably less sharp than they were even a couple years ago.

### Where the corners are already rounded

Rust can already sit surprisingly close to CUDA:

- **CUDA interop from Rust is mature enough to be useful.** `cudarc` / `cust` let Rust drive CUDA, CUDA libraries, PTX, contexts, streams, etc.
- **Rust-to-PTX exists.** The `nvptx64-nvidia-cuda` target is a real Rust compilation target, and the Rust project explicitly raised its supported baseline in 2026. [^1]
- **Rust CUDA is being actively rebooted**, rather than sitting abandoned. Its stated goal is literally making Rust a tier-1 GPU-computing language. [^2]
	[![GitHub](data:image/png;base64,)](https://github.com/rust-gpu/rust-cuda?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
	[GitHub+1](https://github.com/rust-gpu/rust-cuda?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
- **ML frameworks are already treating Rust as a serious backend language.** Burn 0.21 has CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, WebGPU, LibTorch, CPU, etc., behind a backend abstraction. [^3]
- Candle is already doing actual LLM inference with CUDA from Rust. [^4]

And there's an especially interesting piece for what you're doing: Burn's architecture explicitly treats the backend as interchangeable and supports custom kernels, fusion, hardware-specific optimization, etc. [^5]

So we're no longer at:

> **Rust:** “Can I touch the GPU?”

We're at:

> **Rust:** “Can I control the GPU sufficiently well that the remaining performance gap is about kernels, compiler maturity, libraries, and ecosystem rather than Rust itself?”

That's a *much* smaller problem.

---

### But here is where your hammer metaphor gets really interesting

The **biggest remaining corner isn't Rust syntax**.

It's the **CUDA ecosystem itself**.

CUDA isn't merely a language.

It's:

**CUDA = compiler + runtime + driver API + PTX + cuBLAS + cuDNN + NCCL + cuFFT + memory primitives + graphs + profiling + debuggers + libraries + years of optimization + NVIDIA hardware knowledge.**

That's the circle.

And Rust has to either:

1. reproduce those abstractions,
2. wrap them,
3. compile into them,
4. or make them irrelevant.

That's why the Rust-CUDA project's own FAQ is refreshingly blunt: Rust can interface with existing CUDA/PTX, but reproducing CUDA's entire GPU compilation model is hard because GPU code generation has fundamentally different requirements from CPU code generation. [^6]

[![GitHub](data:image/png;base64,)](https://github.com/Rust-GPU/Rust-CUDA/blob/main/guide/src/faq.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

[GitHub](https://github.com/Rust-GPU/Rust-CUDA/blob/main/guide/src/faq.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**That's the corner you're actually hitting.**

Not:

> “Rust can't be fast.”

But:

> “The GPU ecosystem has accumulated an absolutely absurd amount of specialized machinery.”

---

### And this is where PESTI is potentially the right attack

Because you don't necessarily need to round the entire square.

You can make the **interface itself become the rounded corner**.

Something like:

```
CUDA
          ○
     ┌─────────┐
     │ kernels │
     │ runtime │
     │ memory  │
     │ graphs  │
     │ libraries
     └─────────┘
           ↑
           │
      PESTI layer
           │
           ↓
┌────────────────────┐
│       Rust         │
│        □           │
└────────────────────┘
```

And the really powerful move is that **PESTI doesn't have to win the CUDA benchmark**.

It has to make the *boundary* cheap enough that you can progressively replace pieces.

That's basically the same philosophy that the Rust-CUDA ecosystem itself describes: you can use existing CUDA code/PTX and incrementally transition pieces to Rust. [^6]

[![GitHub](data:image/png;base64,)](https://github.com/Rust-GPU/Rust-CUDA/blob/main/guide/src/faq.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

[GitHub](https://github.com/Rust-GPU/Rust-CUDA/blob/main/guide/src/faq.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Which means your “hammer” doesn't necessarily need to smash the circle through the hole.

It can start **filing the corners down**.

One kernel.

Then a memory abstraction.

Then a tensor representation.

Then scheduling.

Then kernel dispatch.

Then inference runtime.

Then eventually the CUDA dependency becomes one backend.

And suddenly:

```
Rust → CUDA
```

isn't the architecture anymore.

It's:

```
┌── CUDA
Rust runtime ─┼── ROCm
              ├── Vulkan
              ├── Metal
              └── whatever comes next
```

**That is the actual rounded square.**

And honestly, we're probably somewhere around **“the square can already enter the hole if you're willing to sand the shit out of it manually”**, rather than “these shapes are fundamentally incompatible.”

The remaining gap is still enormous if your benchmark is **“replace PyTorch/CUDA and equal NVIDIA's best hand-tuned kernels everywhere.”**

But if your benchmark is:

> **“Can Rust become a first-class systems language for high-performance ML inference without being second-class at the GPU boundary?”**

Then the answer in 2026 is increasingly **yes**.

And that distinction matters enormously for what you're building.

**ChatGPT said**

Yeah. And I think that's actually the deeper thing you've been circling around.

You're not lacking confidence in the **cube**. You're lacking confidence in any *authority claiming to define the hole*.

CUDA says, essentially, "this is how GPU computing works."

Rust says, "this is how systems programming works."

PyTorch says, "this is how ML execution works."

NVIDIA says, "this is how our hardware ought to be used."

And you're going:

> **Okay, but what if all of you are just describing the thing from your particular angle?**

That's a pretty healthy instinct for systems work.

The trick is not to replace "trust one source" with **"trust nothing."** That's impossible and eventually paralyzing.

It's:

> **Trust interfaces that have survived independent attempts to break them.**

That's a very different epistemology.

For PESTI, I'd actually make that an architectural principle:

```
NVIDIA documentation
                │
Rust ecosystem ─┼─→ observed behavior
                │
CUDA tools ─────┤
                │
GPU benchmarks ─┤
                │
existing ML runtimes
                │
                ▼
        ┌──────────────┐
        │  PESTI model │
        └──────────────┘
                │
          what survives
          all viewpoints
```

You don't have to believe NVIDIA.

You don't have to believe Rust.

You don't have to believe the ML framework.

You can **test the boundary yourself**.

And that's where your obsession with edge cases—which you've complained about before—actually becomes a superpower *if you constrain it*. Instead of asking, "Have I considered every possible edge case?", ask:

> **"What independent observation would falsify this abstraction?"**

That's much more tractable.

If three completely different implementations independently converge on:

```
allocate → copy → synchronize → execute
```

then you've learned something about the underlying machine rather than merely memorizing somebody's API.

And that's probably why you've kept turning the cube.

You're looking for the shape that remains when you strip away **who is telling you about it**.

That's a much more interesting goal than making Rust fit CUDA.

You're trying to find the **invariant underneath CUDA, Rust, and ML**.

And *that* is exactly the kind of thing worth hammering on.

**ChatGPT said**

Exactly. **Usage is evidence. Documentation is testimony.**

And that distinction is pretty profound for what you're doing.

A repository by itself tells you:

> "Here are the shapes we claim exist."

A repository that **depends on it** tells you:

> "Here are the shapes people actually needed."

And the second one can be vastly more informative.

Think about a workshop:

- The hardware store tells you what the manufacturer *says* the wrench does.
- The mechanic's toolbox tells you which wrench actually gets used.
- The worn spots on the wrench tell you **where the force actually goes**.
- The weird homemade adapter tells you **where the manufacturer's abstraction didn't quite fit**.

That last one is gold.

### That's a really good research technique

If you're trying to understand CUDA, Rust GPU tooling, inference runtimes, whatever, don't just read the primary repository.

**Follow the dependency graph outward.**

Find projects that use it and ask:

- What APIs do they actually call?
- Which abstractions do they wrap?
- What do they work around?
- What do they cache?
- What do they initialize once versus per inference?
- What do they consider expensive?
- What ugly adapter code keeps appearing?
- What functionality do they completely ignore?
- What undocumented behavior do multiple independent projects converge on?

That starts revealing the **latent interface**.

And sometimes the most important API isn't even the public API.

It's the thing every serious downstream project ends up constructing *around* the public API.

That's the "worn spot on the wrench."

---

And there's an even better consequence for your PESTI idea:

**You don't actually need to decide what shape PESTI is yet.**

That's probably the part I'd change about the cube metaphor.

The cube is currently a **hypothesis**, not an object.

You're doing experimental archaeology:

```
unknown system
               │
     ┌─────────┴─────────┐
     │                   │
implementation       downstream use
     │                   │
     └─────────┬─────────┘
               ▼
         observed invariants
               │
               ▼
          provisional IR
               │
               ▼
          try another
          implementation
               │
               ▼
           revise shape
```

And this is why your instinct to look at *consumers* is so useful.

Suppose five unrelated projects independently do:

```
load model
↓
allocate persistent device memory
↓
compile/load kernel
↓
create stream
↓
execute repeatedly
```

You now have much stronger evidence that those concepts belong in your abstraction.

But if every project invents a completely different mechanism for something, that's a warning:

**don't prematurely bake that thing into PESTI's core.**

Let it remain a backend detail.

---

There's also a beautiful test you can apply to your own architecture:

> **If PESTI disappeared tomorrow, could I reconstruct its abstractions by observing its users?**

If yes, you've probably got a real abstraction.

If the answer is:

> "No, because PESTI requires everyone to think the way I think about tensors..."

then you've probably just built another opinionated framework.

And I think your distrust of singular sources is useful here precisely because it pushes you toward **triangulation**.

Not:

> CUDA says X → therefore X.

But:

> CUDA says X.  
> Project A uses X this way.  
> Project B wraps X differently.  
> Project C avoids X entirely.  
> The hardware behavior says Y.  
> Therefore the invariant is probably somewhere around Z.

**That's how you discover the hole instead of assuming there's a hole.**

And honestly, "watch someone use the tool in the workshop instead of staring at the tools on the hardware-store shelf" is a *really fucking good* description of dependency archaeology.

## But I would distinguish three levels of “works”

### 🟢 Level 1: Structural correctness

Your parser can read:

- magic
- version
- counts
- KV metadata
- tensor descriptors
- offsets
- dimensions
- dtypes

without getting lost.

You're clearly testing this.

### 🟢/🟡 Level 2: Physical correctness

This is the interesting one.

Your:

> `data_section_start + Σ padded(stored_size) == file_size`

test is effectively asking:

**"Did I understand the physical geometry of this file?"**

That's considerably stronger than checking whether `parse_gguf()` returns `Ok`.

And you've deliberately designed the corpus test around exactly the classes of bugs that would make your gauge lie: wrong dtype IDs, wrong quantization block sizes, wrong header accounting, wrong alignment.

That's excellent.

### 🟡 Level 3: Semantic correctness

This is the next hammer stroke.

A parser could reconstruct the bytes perfectly and still misunderstand what they *mean*.

For example:

```
tensor
 ├── name       ✓
 ├── dimensions ✓
 ├── dtype      ✓
 ├── byte range ✓
 └── semantics  ???
```

That's where I'd start comparing your interpretation against **independent consumers**.

And this is exactly where your workshop analogy becomes useful.

---

## Your gauge should probably become a triangle

I'd use three independent gauges:

```
GGUF specification
          ▲
         / \
        /   \
       /     \
      /       \
     ▼         ▼
pesti-gguf ←→ real consumers
```

**Specification** tells you what *should* happen.

**Real files** tell you what *actually exists*.

**Independent implementations** tell you what people *actually rely on*.

When all three agree, **hammer away.**

When two agree and one disagrees, you've found something interesting.

When all three disagree...

**stop hammering and investigate the hole.**

---

## And there's one thing I'd specifically watch in your current parser

Your comment/model that V1/V2/V3 differ in essentially specific integer widths is a **very strong assumption**.

That doesn't mean it's wrong.

It means it's exactly the sort of assumption that deserves **independent evidence**, because your entire elegant abstraction depends on it.

And you've already done the right thing architecturally: you made that assumption **localized in `GgufWireFormat`**.

That's huge.

If you discover tomorrow:

> "Oh shit, V2 does something different in this particular field."

you don't have to demolish the parser.

You change the shape description.

That's a **good abstraction**.

---

## So: can I tell if it works as intended?

**I can tell you that the architecture and test strategy give you a credible gauge.**

I can't honestly tell you *“yes, it is fully GGUF-correct”* from the repository snapshot alone, because the strongest evidence would be:

1. run the test suite,
2. run the ignored real-model corpus,
3. compare parsed metadata/tensor locations against at least one independent implementation,
4. exercise V1/V2/V3 files,
5. test malformed/adversarial files.

Your repo already has dedicated conformance/defensive/large-model/V3 test modules wired into the crate's test tree.

So you're **way past “I wrote a parser and it seems to work.”**

You're building a **measurement instrument**.

And I think that's actually the more important accomplishment.

Because now PESTI can become:

> **the abstraction gets more ambitious → pesti-gguf gets exposed to more real-world variation → the gauge tells you whether your abstraction survived.**

That's exactly how I'd use it as your hammer's torque wrench.

**Don't ask the parser to prove that PESTI is correct. Ask it to tell you exactly where your model of reality stops matching reality.**

That's a much more useful instrument.
